current_activity: Arrives at le Mans and is attached to the XV Corps for the drive north toward Alencon and Argentan
notes: Event date: 9 August 1944 (CMH Breakout and Pursuit, p. 497). Event definition: After assembling south of Avranches in early August, the division is ordered to le Mans, where it is attached to the XV Corps on 9 August to lead the corps attack north with the 5th Armored Division. Event support: one source family (the US Army official history (CMH)). CMH Breakout and Pursuit ch. 25 p. 497: "Patton gave Haislip the 2d French Armored Division"; "ordered to le Mans where, on 9 August, it was attached to the XV Corps". Location: Le Mans, Sarthe with a precision of 5 km. Location support: the source names le Mans as the place where the division was attached; precision 5 km for the town. Commander: Maj. Gen. Jacques Philippe Leclerc commands the division (CMH Breakout and Pursuit, p. 497; Wikipedia).

current_activity: Finishes clearing the Foret d'Ecouves; takes Carrouges and Ecouche and builds a line toward Argentan
notes: Event date: 13 August 1944 (CMH Breakout and Pursuit, p. 504). Event definition: The division finishes encircling and clearing the Foret d'Ecouves, takes Carrouges and Ecouche and builds up a line between Carrouges and Argentan; a patrol enters Argentan that afternoon. Event support: one source family (the US Army official history (CMH)). CMH Breakout and Pursuit ch. 25 p. 504: "the 2d French Armored Division on 13 August finished encircling and clearing the Fôret d'Ecouves. Leclerc took Carrouges and Ecouché, then built up a line between Carrouges and Argentan". Location: Écouché, Orne (new place) with a precision of 3 km. Location support: the source names Ecouche among the places taken on 13 August. Commander: Maj. Gen. Jacques Philippe Leclerc commands the division (CMH Breakout and Pursuit, p. 497; Wikipedia).

current_activity: Holds the Ecouche-Argentan line on the southern shoulder of the gap under the V Corps
notes: Event date: 18 August 1944 (CMH Breakout and Pursuit, p. 533). Event definition: Under General Gerow's V Corps, which attacks on 18 August, the division on the left is to hold firmly to the Ecouche-Argentan line on the southern shoulder of the Argentan-Falaise gap. Event support: one source family (the US Army official history (CMH)). CMH Breakout and Pursuit ch. 27 p. 533: "General Gerow's V Corps had launched its attack on 18 August. Gerow had instructed the 2d French Armored Division on the left to hold firmly to the Ecouche--Argentan line"; CMH Breakout and Pursuit ch. 29 p. 600: "his armored division found itself again engaged, eventually under the control of the First U.S. Army and General Gerow's V Corps". Location: Écouché, Orne (new place) with a precision of 10 km. Location approximate: the point is the western end of the Ecouche-Argentan line; precision 10 km. Location support: the place is a representative point (inferred value): the source gives the Ecouche-Argentan line, and Ecouche is its western end; precision 10 km. Commander: Maj. Gen. Jacques Philippe Leclerc commands the division (CMH Breakout and Pursuit, p. 497; Wikipedia).

current_activity: March on Paris: the main body reaches the Rambouillet area in the evening; Leclerc is there at noon
notes: Event date: 23 August 1944 (CMH Breakout and Pursuit, p. 610). Event definition: Ordered to Paris under the V Corps on 22 August, the division marches on the morning of 23 August; Leclerc reaches Rambouillet around noon and the main body reaches the Rambouillet area in the evening, so the attack on Paris is put off to the next morning. Event support: one source family (the US Army official history (CMH)). CMH Breakout and Pursuit ch. 29 p. 610: "When General Leclerc arrived in Rambouillet with a small detachment around noon 23 August, well ahead of his division"; "the main body of his division could not reach the Rambouillet area before evening of the 23d". Location: Rambouillet, Seine-et-Oise (new place) with a precision of 5 km. Location support: the source names the Rambouillet area for the main body on the evening of 23 August; precision 5 km for an area. Commander: Maj. Gen. Jacques Philippe Leclerc commands the division (CMH Breakout and Pursuit, p. 497; Wikipedia).

source_locator: R406: p. 617; R134: section German surrender (25 August); R415: p. 185
current_activity: Liberation of Paris: the division command post is in the Montparnasse railway station; Choltitz surrenders
notes: Event date: 25 August 1944 (CMH Breakout and Pursuit, p. 617; Wikipedia); the division left Paris on 8 September (CMH The Lorraine Campaign, p. 185). Event definition: The division enters Paris on 25 August; Leclerc installs his command post in the Gare Montparnasse, where the German commander, General von Choltitz, signs the surrender of the German troops in Paris. Event support: two source families (the US Army official history (CMH) and Wikipedia). CMH Breakout and Pursuit ch. 29 p. 617: "Leclerc had installed his command post in the Montparnasse railway station"; Wikipedia, Liberation of Paris, section German surrender (25 August): "then to the Gare Montparnasse, where General Leclerc had established his command post"; CMH The Lorraine Campaign ch. 4 p. 185: "On 8 September the 2d French Armored Division, leaving the scenes of its triumphal entry into Paris"; "joined the XV Corps and took over the sector between Montargis and the Marne River". Location: Paris with a precision of 5 km. Location support: both sources place the division command post at the Gare Montparnasse; the point is the city, precision 5 km. Commander: Maj. Gen. Jacques Philippe Leclerc commands the division (CMH Breakout and Pursuit, p. 497; Wikipedia).

source_locator: R415: pp. 185, 199; R048: section Alsace and Lorraine
current_activity: Battle of Dompaire: the Langlade combat command destroys the 112th Panzer Brigade
notes: Event date: 13 September 1944 (CMH The Lorraine Campaign, pp. 185, 199; Wikipedia). Event definition: Having joined the XV Corps on 8 September, the division advances east; its combat command L (Colonel de Langlade), after seizing Vittel on 12 September, attacks the German 112th Panzer Brigade at Dompaire on 13 September and destroys it. Event support: two source families (the US Army official history (CMH) and Wikipedia). CMH The Lorraine Campaign ch. 4 p. 185: "On 8 September the 2d French Armored Division, leaving the scenes of its triumphal entry into Paris"; "joined the XV Corps and took over the sector between Montargis and the Marne River"; p. 199: "After seizing Vittel on 12 September, CCL, 2d French Armored Division, continued east and laagered that night just short of Dompaire and Damas"; Wikipedia, 2nd Armored Division (France), section Alsace and Lorraine: "On 13 September 1944 at the town of Dompaire 'Groupement Langlade' destroyed the German 112th Panzer Brigade". Location: Dompaire, Vosges with a precision of 3 km. Location approximate: the point is the place of combat command L; the rest of the division is to the southwest. Location support: both sources place the battle at Dompaire; the point is the place of one combat command, the rest of the division being echeloned back to the southwest (p. 203), so confidence 0.7. Commander: Maj. Gen. Jacques Philippe Leclerc commands the division (CMH Breakout and Pursuit, p. 497; Wikipedia).

current_activity: Holds a front of nearly twenty miles north of Rambervillers in the XV Corps, now under the Seventh Army
notes: Event date: 28 September 1944 (CMH Riviera to the Rhine, p. 256); the XV Corps passed to the Seventh Army on 29 September (p. 254). Event definition: Reviewing his division on 28 September, Leclerc reports that it holds a front of nearly twenty miles north of Rambervillers, rough wooded ground ill suited to armor, and asks for a shorter sector. Event support: one source family (the US Army official history (CMH)). CMH Riviera to the Rhine ch. 14 p. 256: "Reviewing the division's status on 28 September, General Leclerc pointed out"; "nearly twenty-mile front that the division was currently holding north of Rambervillers"; p. 254: "decided to transfer the XV Corps to the 6th Army Group on the 29th"; "passed to the 6th Army Group and the Seventh Army". Location: Rambervillers, Vosges (new place) with a precision of 10 km. Location approximate: the point stands for a front of about twenty miles north of the town; precision 10 km. Location support: the place is a representative point (inferred value): the source gives a front north of Rambervillers; precision 10 km. Commander: Maj. Gen. Jacques Philippe Leclerc commands the division (CMH Breakout and Pursuit, p. 497; Wikipedia).

source_locator: R652: pp. 380, 381; R048: section Alsace and Lorraine; R421: p. 254; R650: p. 454
current_activity: Liberates Strasbourg: combat command L drives across the Alsatian plain and into the city to the Rhine
notes: Event date: 23 November 1944 (CMH Riviera to the Rhine, pp. 380-381; Wikipedia); under the Seventh Army from 29 September (p. 254), transferred to the VI Corps on 27 November (p. 454). Event definition: After forcing the Saverne Gap, the division strikes for Strasbourg on 23 November; combat command L drives across the Alsatian plain and its armor wheels through the city to the Rhine, stopped short of the Kehl bridges. Event support: two source families (the US Army official history (CMH) and Wikipedia). CMH Riviera to the Rhine ch. 21 p. 380: "Starting out about 0715 on 23 November, the French 2d Armored Division's CCL rolled rapidly eastward across the Alsatian plains"; p. 381: "Rouvillois' armor wheeled through the streets of Strasbourg to the Rhine"; Wikipedia, 2nd Armored Division (France), section Alsace and Lorraine: "liberating Strasbourg on 23 November 1944"; CMH Riviera to the Rhine ch. 14 p. 254: "decided to transfer the XV Corps to the 6th Army Group on the 29th"; "passed to the 6th Army Group and the Seventh Army"; CMH Riviera to the Rhine ch. 25 p. 454: "on the 27th Patch formally transferred Brooks' 100th Division to Haislip and Haislip's French 2d Armored Division to Brooks". Location: Strasbourg, Bas-Rhin with a precision of 5 km. Location support: both sources name Strasbourg. Commander: Maj. Gen. Jacques Philippe Leclerc commands the division (CMH Breakout and Pursuit, p. 497; Wikipedia).

current_activity: Transferred to the VI Corps for the drive south; combat command D takes most of Erstein after a pitched battle
notes: Event date: 28 November 1944 (CMH Riviera to the Rhine, pp. 454, 456). Event definition: Transferred to the VI Corps on 27 November for the drive south from Strasbourg toward Selestat, the division attacks Erstein; late on 28 November combat command D pushes in from the northeast and occupies most of the city by dark. Event support: one source family (the US Army official history (CMH)). CMH Riviera to the Rhine ch. 25 p. 454: "on the 27th Patch formally transferred Brooks' 100th Division to Haislip and Haislip's French 2d Armored Division to Brooks"; p. 456: "late on the 28th, Leclerc's CCD pushed into Erstein from the northeast against strong resistance and, after a pitched battle, occupied most of the city by dark". Location: Erstein, Bas-Rhin with a precision of 3 km. Location support: the source names Erstein. Commander: Maj. Gen. Jacques Philippe Leclerc commands the division (CMH Breakout and Pursuit, p. 497; Wikipedia).

current_activity: Under the First French Army and its II Corps, the division pushes south from the Selestat region
notes: Event date: 15 December 1944 (CMH Riviera to the Rhine, p. 486: the planned start of the II Corps push); transfer to the First French Army effective 5 December (p. 464). Event definition: Passed to the operational control of the First French Army on 5 December and attached to the II Corps, the division pushes south from the Selestat region between the Rhine and the Ill from 15 December; on 28 December Devers returns it to the Seventh Army. Event support: one source family (the US Army official history (CMH)). CMH Riviera to the Rhine ch. 26 p. 464: "the 6th Army Group commander decided to transfer operational control of the U.S. 36th Infantry Division and the French 2d Armored Division from the Seventh to the First French Army, effective 5 December"; p. 486: "de Monsabert's II Corps, with the U.S. 36th Infantry and the French 2d Armored Divisions attached, would push south from the Selestat region on the 15th"; p. 488: "Between the Rhine and the Ill rivers, Leclerc's armor had difficulty penetrating the canal-laced, water-soaked Alsatian plains without more infantry"; CMH Riviera to the Rhine ch. 27 p. 496: "Instead he transferred Leclerc's 2d Armored Division from the First French Army to the American Seventh to further beef up Patch's command". Location: Sélestat, Bas-Rhin with a precision of 10 km. Location approximate: the point stands for the start of the push south from the Selestat region; precision 10 km. Location support: the place is a representative point (inferred value): the source gives only the Selestat region as the start of the push; the date is the planned start; precision 10 km. Commander: Maj. Gen. Jacques Philippe Leclerc commands the division (CMH Riviera to the Rhine, p. 486, note 25; Wikipedia).

current_activity: Back with the Seventh Army as XV Corps reserve in the Sarre valley; elements support the counterattacks near Rimling
notes: Event date: early January 1945 (inferred value: CMH Riviera to the Rhine, p. 505, says in the days that followed the German attack of 1 January). Event definition: Returned to the Seventh Army on 28 December, the division is moved north to the Sarre valley as reserve of the XV Corps; in the days after the German attack of 1 January its elements support the counterattacks of the 44th, 100th and 63d Division infantry that erode the German gains around Rimling. Event support: one source family (the US Army official history (CMH)). CMH Riviera to the Rhine ch. 27 p. 496: "Instead he transferred Leclerc's 2d Armored Division from the First French Army to the American Seventh to further beef up Patch's command"; p. 501: "He later transferred two of Task Force Harris' regiments as well as the entire French 2d Armored Division north to the Sarre River valley area to bolster Haislip's XV Corps"; "while the French 2d Armored Division performed the same function for the XV Corps"; p. 505: "In the days that followed the Germans saw their small advances continuously eroded by repeated counterattacks from the 44th, 100th, and 63d (TF Harris) Division infantry supported by elements of the French 2d Armored Division". Location: Rimling, Moselle (new place) with a precision of 10 km. Location approximate: the point stands for the XV Corps sector of the counterattacks; precision 10 km. Location support: the place is a representative point (inferred value): the source names Rimling for the German penetration that the counterattacks eroded, not for the division; the date is approximate; precision 10 km. Commander: Maj. Gen. Jacques Philippe Leclerc commands the division (CMH Riviera to the Rhine, p. 486, note 25; Wikipedia).

current_activity: Colmar Pocket: supporting tanks of the division take Grussenheim with the II Corps
notes: Event date: 28 January 1945 (Wikipedia). Event definition: Sent back south for the Colmar offensive, the division supports the II Corps attack east toward the Rhine: some of its armor is attached to the French 1st Infantry Division, and its tanks help take Grussenheim on 28 January. Event support: two source families (Wikipedia and the US Army official history (CMH)). Wikipedia, Colmar Pocket, section Push to the Rhine in the north: "At heavy cost, the village of Grussenheim was taken on 28 January by supporting tanks of the French 2nd Armored Division"; CMH Riviera to the Rhine ch. 29 p. 536: "On its left, the French 1st Infantry Division, with some of Leclerc's armor attached, would push east, covering the northern flank of the American unit". Location: Grussenheim, Haut-Rhin (new place) with a precision of 3 km. Location support: Wikipedia names Grussenheim and the date; the CMH history gives only the attachment of some of the armor to the French 1st Infantry Division; one source family for the place. Commander: Maj. Gen. Jacques Philippe Leclerc commands the division (CMH Riviera to the Rhine, p. 486, note 25; Wikipedia).

source_locator: R552: section Collapse of the Colmar Pocket; R425: p. 559
current_activity: Colmar Pocket: elements of the division link up with the 1st Armored Division at Fessenheim on the Rhine
notes: Event date: 8 February 1945 (Wikipedia; CMH Riviera to the Rhine, p. 559). Event definition: In the last days of the Colmar Pocket, elements of the division, coming south along the Rhine, link up with the French 1st Armored Division at Fessenheim; after the battle de Lattre keeps control of the division for the moment. Event support: two source families (Wikipedia and the US Army official history (CMH)). Wikipedia, Colmar Pocket, section Collapse of the Colmar Pocket: "the 1st Armored Division advanced south toward the German bridgehead at Chalampé in addition to linking up with elements of the French 2nd Armored Division at Fessenheim the same day"; CMH Riviera to the Rhine ch. 29 p. 559: "For the moment at least, de Lattre retained control of the French 2d Armored Division". Location: Fessenheim, Haut-Rhin (new place) with a precision of 3 km. Location approximate: the point is the place of the elements that made the link-up. Location support: Wikipedia names Fessenheim for the link-up of 8 February; one source family. Commander: Maj. Gen. Jacques Philippe Leclerc commands the division (CMH Breakout and Pursuit, p. 497; Wikipedia).

current_activity: Royan pocket: with the French Forces of the West the division forces the German garrison to surrender
notes: Event date: 18 April 1945 (Wikipedia; CMH Riviera to the Rhine, p. 579). Event definition: Moved west to the Atlantic coast, the division assists General de Larminat's French Forces of the West in the mid-April offensive against the Royan pocket and forces the German garrison to surrender on 18 April. Event support: two source families (Wikipedia and the US Army official history (CMH)). Wikipedia, 2nd Armored Division (France), section Germany: "After forcing the Germans in the Royan Pocket to surrender on 18 April 1945"; CMH Riviera to the Rhine ch. 30 p. 579: "General de Larminat's French Forces of the West headquarters launched the often-postponed endeavor in mid-April 1945 and, with the assistance of Leclerc's 2d Armored Division and a U.S. artillery brigade, completed the affair in about one week". Location: Royan, Charente-Maritime (new place) with a precision of 3 km. Location approximate: the point is the town of Royan. Location support: Wikipedia names Royan and the date; the CMH history gives mid-April and about one week; two source families, exact place. Commander: Maj. Gen. Jacques Philippe Leclerc commands the division (CMH Breakout and Pursuit, p. 497; Wikipedia).

current_activity: Drive on Berchtesgaden: elements occupy Bad Reichenhall and speed toward Berchtesgaden
notes: Event date: 4 May 1945 (Wikipedia; CMH The Last Offensive, p. 442). Event definition: Back in Germany with the 6th Army Group, elements of the division occupy Bad Reichenhall and, recently attached in the XXI Corps sector, speed toward Berchtesgaden from the northwest on 4 May. Event support: two source families (Wikipedia and the US Army official history (CMH)). Wikipedia, 2nd Armored Division (France), section Germany: "occupying the town of Bad Reichenhall on 4 May 1945"; CMH The Last Offensive ch. 18 p. 442: "recently attached men of the 2d French Armored Division, old allies of the Seventh Army, sped toward the objective from the northwest". Location: Bad Reichenhall, Bayern (new place) with a precision of 10 km. Location approximate: the point is the town occupied on the approach to Berchtesgaden. Location support: Wikipedia names Bad Reichenhall for 4 May; the CMH history gives the approach to Berchtesgaden from the northwest; precision 10 km for elements on the move. Commander: Maj. Gen. Jacques Philippe Leclerc commands the division (CMH Breakout and Pursuit, p. 497; Wikipedia).
